name: wrought_iron
summary: Railings and gates: bar iron drawn out under a hammer, spear-topped, and left to weather black.
why: Metallic 1.0, which is the argument worth having. Every other dark surface in this library
is a dielectric and this one is not: MU draws a bright highlight straight down each bar,
which is what bare metal does and what paint does not. Painted railings would want metallic
0 and a mid roughness, and would come out looking like plastic rod.
Roughness 0.50, smoother than plate_steel's 0.68 and rougher than a blade's 0.32. A railing
is drawn under a hammer rather than cast, so it has none of plate's pitting, and it is left
in the rain for years, so it has none of a blade's polish. The number sits between the two
materials it sits between physically.
Cast grain rather than brushed, at scale 240. Drawn bar has a direction and it is the wrong
one to emphasise: the bars are vertical and a brushed normal running up them would put
parallel scratches down a surface whose whole read is its silhouette against the sky.
Depth 0.18, modest. What a railing has is shape, not texture - 85% of its sheet is cut away
and the eye reads the gap between the bars. Relief on the bar itself is a detail nobody
gets close enough to see.
It always arrives with a cut-out. steel_barred_a cuts away 85% of its square and the gate
43%: these are shapes made of alpha, like the foliage, and unlike the foliage they are
solid and want their normals left alone.
It stays metallic 1.0 even though the same measurement that condemned painted_steel
condemns this: steel_barred_a is 0.066 in linear where iron's reflectance is 0.56, so as a
metal it is darker than any that exists. Tested rather than argued - the railing rendered
both ways, side by side. At metallic 1 it is black iron, which is what a garden railing is.
At metallic 0 it is pale brass rod, which is not.
The difference from painted_steel is what the art is doing, not what its average is.
steel.jpg is a bright highlight painted down a blade and its darkness is the *background*
to that highlight; treated as metal the highlight goes and the background is all that is
left. Here the darkness is the subject - these are bars painted black - and treating them
as a very dark metal gives exactly the sky-edged silhouette the thing has in life.
So two materials for MU's metal, and the line between them is whether the dark in the sheet
is the thing or the absence of the thing.

f0 0.52, and it had none - the second metal found stating metallic 1.0 with no reflectance to state, after brass. base_colour skips a metal without one, so the renderer read MU's painted sheet as reflectance. Measured on the Crossbow the albedo and the basecolor are the same numbers to three places, (0.329, 0.400, 0.333): green, at a third of the light iron returns. Iron's published base colour sits near (0.56, 0.57, 0.58); 0.52 is a little under it because wrought iron is worked and weathered rather than polished bar, and under steel's 0.56 for the same reason.

f0_desaturation 0.60, which is the strongest pull in the library and the opposite of the decision brass took. The two cases are the test of that knob: brass gets none because a brass that is not yellow is not brass, and iron gets a hard one because an iron that is green is not iron. The green here is MU painting a shadowed prod against foliage, not the metal's own colour - the sheet is a picture of light, which is exactly the case f0_desaturation was written for. f0_from_art 0.4 rather than 0.5 for the same reason: less of that painting is about the surface.

Grain depth 0.18 -> 0.06, the third material to take this correction after bone and brass and the worst of them. It gave the Crossbow's prod a normal deviation of 0.164, the highest measured anywhere in the project, and drove specular_floor to push roughness to 1.00 against the 0.50 this file asks for. Wrought iron is hammered and should carry more texture than rolled steel's 0.01 - 0.06 keeps that and stops it being noise.
